chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
title: Palm Garden in Milwaukee and a prejudiced owner
summary: A prejudiced owner kept the band away from patrons until a friend threatened him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Then I went to Milwaukee to play at the Palm Garden; Rozelle Claxton I guess, Kansas Fields, Dave Young, John Simmons on bass, and myself -- five pieces. That was a

funny job, too, because this cat here wwas a very prejudiced cat. He didn't allow the band to come out behind the bandstand. No, you had to go down through a trap door down to the basement. You would go out the back door to the bus station(?). Them bars wasn't too cool in those days either, you know.

But I had a friend who was a pretty rough character, you know. In fact, he took a gun off a cat in there one night. This cat was kind of scary(?). So he came in to see me, because he used to me when I was in the Deuces, you know... He come in to see me one night, and he said, "Come on and have a drink." I said, "This cat don't let me (?) to have a drink." "What?" So he called him, "Hey, Mister Dishrag! This cat told me... You know, Roy is my boy, man, and I want him out here to drink with me." Oh yeah, of course." And he opened up the... "Roy's fine with me. He's doing a good job." He said, "Don't give me that shit. Stop putting pressure on him. If he wants to come out and drink with people, let him drink. If he tells me anything happens different, I'm going to come down and know why." From then on, I had no problem with him.
I had the same thing happen when Artie Shaw came down; I had a drink with him, too.
